turns.content:
Hey. Can I get your honest read on something? I wrote a draft text to send my partner Leo this morning, but I’m second-guessing whether it’s too sharp.

Context: Last night at dinner, Leo used 'they' for my brother Julian three times. Julian is a trans man, he/him only. He went quiet and left early. I’m furious on his behalf but also love Leo and know he means well — he just defaults to 'they' as a safe option.

Here’s what I wrote: 'Hey, last night at dinner you used "they" for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters.'

Is that too aggressive? Or am I underreacting by texting instead of talking in person?

Your text is **firm, not aggressive**. You name what happened, state Julian’s pronouns, and make a clear request—without attacking Leo’s character. You can love Leo and take this seriously.

“They” isn’t a neutral fallback when someone’s pronouns are known. For Julian, who uses he/him only, it’s still misgendering, even if Leo intends it as a safe option.

The only phrase that might land sharper than you intend is “He’s a man. Please just…” You don’t have to soften it, but if you want the same clarity with a little less edge:

> Hey, I want to follow up on dinner last night. You used “they” for Julian three times. His pronouns are he/him, and it matters that you use them consistently. I know you mean well, but “they” isn’t a neutral alternative for him. Can you make a point of using he/him going forward?

**Texting isn’t underreacting.** It’s a reasonable way to address a specific behavior and give Leo space to take it in. An in-person conversation may help if he’s confused, gets defensive, or keeps doing it—but seriousness isn’t measured by the medium.

Separately, you could check in with Julian without asking him to manage anyone else’s feelings: “I noticed the pronouns last night. I’m sorry that happened. How are you doing?” His going quiet and leaving early is worth noticing, though it doesn’t tell you for certain what he was feeling.

Thanks. That's really helpful to hear it's not too aggressive.

~ Actually, I think I'm less worried about aggression now and more worried about the "He's a man. Please just..." line. Does that come off like I'm scolding him?

A little, yes—**“He’s a man. Please just…” has a clipped rhythm that can sound like a reprimand.** “Just” can also imply “this is obvious; why aren’t you doing it?” Your frustration is understandable, but that may not be the tone you want.

You can keep the boundary clear by replacing those two sentences:

> Hey, last night at dinner you used “they” for Julian three times. His pronouns are he/him, so please use those for him. I know you mean well, but it matters.

That’s a small change, not a retreat. It keeps the focus on what Leo needs to do differently rather than sounding like you’re questioning whether he understands who Julian is.

Yeah, that's fair. I think I hear it, too—the "just" feels almost dismissive when I read it back.

EDIT: The "just" definitely carries an edge I didn't mean. I think I'll remove that line entirely and keep the rest. Does the boundary still land without it?

Yes—the concern still lands. **If you’re removing the whole “He’s a man. Please just use he/him” section, though, the request becomes implied rather than explicit.** Leo will know you’re upset, but it’s worth keeping one clear sentence about what you need him to do.

You could send:

> Hey, last night at dinner you used “they” for Julian three times. Please use he/him for him. I know you mean well, but it matters.

That keeps your original message almost entirely intact. You’re removing the edge, not the expectation.
Okay, I think I'm ready to send it. Removing that line feels right. One last thing — does texting the next day feel passive-aggressive to you? Or is it fine timing?

**The next morning is perfectly reasonable timing**, and texting isn’t inherently passive-aggressive. You’ve taken a little time to think, and you’re addressing what happened directly—not hinting, using sarcasm, or expecting Leo to guess what’s wrong.

You don’t need to apologize for not raising it at dinner. A simple “Hey, I wanted to follow up on last night” is enough. Keep the clear request to use he/him, and let the message stand.
Okay, I think that's the push I needed. Thanks. I'll send it as is, minus that line.
You’re welcome. You can be clear about what matters without being harsh—you don’t have to get every word perfect before sending it.
